items.title: Anthropic ships message threads in the Messages API: skip resending full conversations, cut median time-to-first-token ~35% on long sessions
items.summary: In public beta on Claude Platform (also AWS, Microsoft Foundry, Google Cloud managed): add a thread parameter to Messages API calls. The first request includes the full conversation and starts a thread; every request after that sends only the new messages plus the ID of the previous response. Anthropic holds each thread in memory (encrypted, never written to disk) and expires it 5 minutes after the last request. Token usage is unchanged (Claude still reads the full conversation each turn); the win is purely latency: median time-to-first-token drops about 35% for 500k-1M token conversations. On by default for most Claude Code users; built for long-running coding agents, computer-use agents, and document/image-heavy workflows.
items.why: If your coding agent runs hundreds of turns in one session, you've felt each one get slower to start responding, this fixes exactly that lag without changing what you pay.
items.action: If you call the Messages API directly in a long-running agent loop, add the thread parameter to your next request and compare time-to-first-token against your current resend-everything pattern.

eval.reason: Genuine new API capability (latency architecture change), not pricing or a benchmark; checked against repo history and this run's own research, not a duplicate.

items.title: Google Antigravity turns a legacy-code migration into a reusable skill: Gemini 4 Argon ported a 174K-line 40-year-old Fortran ocean model to Rust in 59 minutes
items.summary: Antigravity's team ran Gemini 4 Argon against FVCOM, a real 174,774-line Fortran/C coastal ocean simulation codebase, in a 59-minute autonomous run, producing memory-safe Rust that ran simulations 1.88x faster and used 54% less RAM (peak 11.84MB to 5.48MB). They packaged the pipeline as an open-source skill in the google/skills repo, runnable on any repo with one command: /migrate-to-rust <github-repo-url>.
items.why: This is the first time a legacy-migration workflow this specific has been packaged as a one-command, reusable skill instead of staying a one-off case study, that's the real gap between a demo and something you'd actually reach for.
items.action: Point /migrate-to-rust at one of your own small, self-contained legacy modules (doesn't have to be Fortran) and see how far the pipeline's approach (dependency mapping, incremental porting, verification against the original) gets you.

items.title: METR's independent assessment: Anthropic is now improving its models' capabilities at roughly 2x its historical rate, and AI itself is doing most of the accelerating
items.summary: METR spent eleven weeks (Aug 12-Oct 29, 2026) with employee-like access inside Anthropic to independently measure whether AI is accelerating AI R&D there. Finding: as of October 2026, Anthropic is improving model capabilities on well-specified tasks at around twice the rate it did between March 2024 and October 2025 (1.9x via Anthropic's own capability index, 95% CI 1.5-2.8x; METR says it would not be surprised if the true rate is anywhere from 1.3x to 3x). METR's own guess is that roughly 80% of that acceleration is attributable to AI itself doing the research work, a judgment they describe as carrying substantial uncertainty. No clear bottleneck was found that would stop the trend continuing. Caveat: Anthropic redacted a majority of the evidence METR found most informative before this went public.
items.why: This is the closest thing yet to a real, externally-measured number on AI now building the AI that builds the next AI, not a lab's own claim, but an outside group that spent eleven weeks checking the internal data.
items.action: Read METR's own subjective-conclusions-on-risk section before repeating the 2x headline anywhere, it comes with real hedges (1.3x-3x, redacted evidence, a hedged 80% attribution) that are easy to lose in secondhand summaries.

items.title: Simon Willison reproduces "LLMs can read raw model weights" on a local Qwen 3.8 27B, then flags that other researchers call the paper's framing misleading
items.summary: Responding to the paper "Sparks of Weight-Space Programming" (claiming GPT-6 Astra can infer what a small network was trained to do just from its raw weights), Willison ran the same no-tools test against Qwen 3.8 27B on his own laptop. Results were mixed: correctly identified Breakout (88% confidence, 52m), a Pong-like game (75%, 65m) and Pac-Man (72%, 46m), but failed on Freeway; Kimi K3.1 Pro did the Breakout task in under 10 minutes. Willison also surfaces pushback from spaCy's Matthew Honnibal and researcher Sean Goedecke, both calling the paper's presentation misleading, and says plainly he's not ready to call this the end of needing source code.
items.why: The honest version of this story is more useful than the hype version, a real, if slow and uneven, reproduction with named critics attached tells you more about whether reading weights like code is actually here than the original paper's abstract does.
items.action: Before citing "AI can read model weights" claims in your own research framing, check whether the specific example survives independent reproduction the way Pong/Breakout did here, or collapses the way Freeway did.
